Talking with others about the event or its aftermath

When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
There is something wrong with me as a person

vignette: Amina is a 25-year-old African-American nurse who has been living with the aftermath of her experiences in a war-torn region where she served as a volunteer aid worker. The traumatic event that continues to haunt her occurred one night when the hospital where she worked was shelled, leaving several patients and colleagues dead or injured. She remembers the explosions tearing through the building like punches of terror, each blast echoing with the weight of lives lost. The memory is visceral, replaying in her mind as if it were happening right now. When these memories return, Amina feels so overwhelmed by emotion that she has to stop whatever she’s doing and retreat into herself. This reliving of the event often leads her to drift off into a world of her own, where she can momentarily escape from the overwhelming grief and fear. Talking about what happened is almost unbearable; it feels like reopening old wounds that have never truly healed. Amina has come to believe that there is something wrong with her as a person. She feels permanently humiliated by the events of that night, and this sense of inadequacy only deepens each time she relives the trauma in her mind. The memory often triggers these feelings, reinforcing her negative appraisals about herself and leading her to withdraw further into fantasy escape or silence. Her maladaptive strategies have become a coping mechanism for dealing with the overwhelming emotions that arise from the memories. Amina finds solace in drifting away into her own world of imagination, allowing her mind to take refuge where it’s safer than reality. Avoiding conversations about the event or its aftermath is another way she copes; talking about it makes her feel more inadequate and flawed. Her avoidance has consequences that extend beyond just emotional isolation. As a nurse, Amina finds herself struggling to engage fully with patients and colleagues who have their own stories of trauma. Her reluctance to speak openly impacts her ability to form deep connections at work, leading to moments where she feels further isolated and less effective in her role. Amina’s avoidance behaviors also extend into her personal life. She avoids situations or conversations that might trigger memories of the war zone, creating a sense of distance between herself and her partner. The grief on recall is intense, and the feeling of being overwhelmed emotionally can be paralyzing. Each time she experiences this overwhelm, it reinforces her negative appraisals and leads to more pronounced avoidance behaviors. The loop tightens as Amina’s memories trigger these overwhelming emotions, pushing her further into isolation and self-doubt. She drifts off into a world of her own not just to escape the present but also to shield herself from the memories that haunt her. This cycle has been escalating over time, making it increasingly difficult for her to function both professionally and personally. What finally brought Amina to seek help was a realization that these behaviors were impacting every aspect of her life. She fears being stuck in this cycle forever, unable to connect with others or find peace within herself. Despite the overwhelming feelings she experiences, there is also a glimmer of hope that through therapy, she might be able to regain some sense of control and start healing from the trauma. Amina’s most profound fear is feeling permanently flawed, but her deepest hope is to break free from this cycle and reclaim a life where she can fully engage with those around her without being consumed by the memories of war.
